transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-15 16:30 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Imani (Redwood Infra), Raj (Nova platform), Elena (Nova SRE), Tom (CTO), Lina (Security)
---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, is the audio good?
[00:06] Raj: Yeah, lgtm. Thanks Maya. We wanted this to be very technical — we saw p99 spikes in prod over last week.
[00:12] Diego: Cool. We got the perf logs you attached, thanks. We'll walk through the hypothesis: multi-hop networking + cold KV cache + batching edge cases. We'll demo microbench numbers at the end.
[00:25] Elena: To scope it, our setup is 3 AZs in MajorCloudX, VPC peering to our on-prem via a bastion NAT, TLS termination at the bastion, and then a private line to the inference pool. Most inference calls go through a proxy on-prem for auditing which adds a hop.
[00:40] Imani: That topology already rings bell bells — every additional hop increases handshake and jitter risk, plus if you cross NAT, you can see connection churn affecting streaming keepalive.
[00:50] Tom: The numbers: p95 around 120ms, p99 around 540ms at times. During batch windows we get lower median but spikes remain. We saw p99 coincide with heavy KV misses flagged by our cache logs.
[01:05] Diego: Okay that's a good signal. A typical pattern we see is: request arrives -> prefix not cached -> runtime does KV lookup behind the model shard -> that lookup either hits a remote KV store (cross-AZ) or pulls from disk when cold -> while waiting, streaming connections may keep open but timeouts/keepalive cause chunking and extra retransmits.
[01:28] Raj: We use a managed Redis in another region with replication; replication lag can add 50-200ms sometimes. Could that be the culprit?
[01:35] Diego: Possibly. If the KV cache is remote, misses cost network RTTs. Also our runtime's continuous batching can hold short windows to fill batches which can add a few ms intentionally, but when combined with remote KV miss it compounds.
[01:50] Elena: We tried reducing batch windows but then saw throughput drop. It's a tradeoff.
[01:55] Maya: Let's break down the likely contributors: (1) network hops and TLS handshake (bastion/NAT), (2) remote KV latency and cold misses, (3) batching policy and interaction with streaming, (4) quantization/CPU decoding slow paths for small batch sizes.
[02:10] Lina: From a security angle, we need audit + TLS at the bastion, can't remove that hop. But if we can reduce its impact that's better.
[02:22] Diego: A few immediate tuning items: enable persistent keep-alive for streaming (reduce handshake count), set shorter batch windows but enable adaptive batching (reduce p95 without hurting p50), and warm the KV cache by prefetching hot prefixes.
[02:37] Raj: Prefetching sounds good, but how do we identify hot prefixes? Our workload is mixed — a few hot prompt templates plus a long tail.
[02:45] Diego: We instrument token prefix histograms; Redwood Console has a hot-prefix detector. We can share a script to generate a top-N prefix list and a warm-up task to push those prefixes into runtime cache on startup.
[02:58] Elena: What about streaming vs non-streaming? We noticed streaming reduces median but sometimes increases p99 when networks jitter.
[03:06] Diego: Streaming can help because partial tokens are streamed out as soon as they're produced — that helps perceived latency. But it keeps connections open longer; if there's a mid-response packet loss or TCP stall behind a NAT, the tail can blow up. Non-streaming (full response) hides token-by-token jitter at the cost of higher median. So it depends on network stability and where the churn occurs.
[03:28] Imani: Also consider HTTP/2 multiplexing vs gRPC vs QUIC. We've seen QUIC reduce handshake overhead for short-lived connections — but it's not always available in managed infra.
[03:40] Tom: Could you explain where kernel selection and quantization play in? We tried an int8 config that lowered token cost but had weird slowdowns occasionally.
[03:49] Diego: Sure. Quantization reduces memory bandwidth and inference CPU, but some kernels for int8 have slower decode paths when sequence lengths are small — vRNN-style kernels can be suboptimal for small batch small seq. That can create microseconds-per-token regressions that add up into p99 when compounded with network jitter. Also, some quantized paths force more CPU spinning on re-ordering which interacts poorly with kernel scheduling under Linux cgroups.
[04:16] Raj: So recommended approach?
[04:18] Diego: For Nova's profile (mixed hot prefixes + long tail), we recommend: keep streaming enabled for hot-paths (hot prefix detection), use prefix prefetch to populate KV cache, route cold-paths to a slightly larger batch size non-stream path to smooth out per-token overhead, and ensure KV store is cross-AZ replicated with read replicas local to inference AZs when possible.
[04:41] Maya: We'll share a sample routing policy: hot-prefix => streaming, small-batch window (e.g., 8-12ms), cold-prefix => non-streaming, batch up to N=8 or N=16 depending on throughput. Also an automatic fallback to local quantized model variant if remote variant not available.
[05:00] Elena: We saw a case where a single bad hop (bastion) caused p99 to jump to 1.2s for some requests. Any way to detect that quickly?
[05:09] Imani: Yes, trace IDs across the whole path (edge proxy -> bastion -> inference) with per-hop timings in the trace. If you instrument TCP/TLS handshake times and measure per-hop latency from the trace, you can correlate p99 to a particular hop. eBPF tcp_probe or netstat-level logs help.
[05:28] Raj: We'll collect traceroutes and tcpdump for a few p99 samples.
[05:32] Diego: Perfect. Also, when you share traces, highlight the KV miss vs hit. We had one case where a p99 lined up exactly with a KV miss that then triggered disk paging on the model shard — ugly stack.
[05:45] Tom: The model shards are pinned to GPUs in a Dedicated-like pool. Do you recommend moving them into AZ-local pools?
[05:52] Diego: Yes. AZ-local inference pools minimize cross-AZ RTTs. If you're running on a dedicated cluster, try to collocate KV replicas in the same AZ or use a memory-attached cache co-located with the runtime.
[06:03] Maya: Quick demo: Diego ran a small lab earlier — numbers: baseline median 70ms, p95 140ms, p99 560ms. With hot-prefix prefetch + streaming keepalive tweaks p95 dropped to 110ms and p99 to 230ms in the same topology. When we forced an extra NAT hop in the lab p99 climbed back to ~620ms.
[06:28] Elena: That aligns with our experience. The NAT keeps state and sometimes drops connections causing reconnection cost.
[06:35] Raj: Any recommended batch tuning? We saw that decreasing batch window from 25ms to 8ms helped median but hurt throughput.
[06:42] Diego: Try dynamic windowing: set a small target window (8-12ms) but let the server increase the window adaptively if throughput drops below threshold. Also use micro-batching: continuously flush partial batches for streaming hot-paths while allowing non-streaming cold-paths to accumulate.
[07:00] Lina: From security, we need audit logs retained 1 year and key rotation — does enabling prefix prefetch or caching expose new data residency concerns?
[07:09] Maya: Prefetch only stores the prefix hashes in runtime memory — no PII should be stored. But we'll document exactly what is cached and provide the dataflow diagram. We'll also provide KMS/HSM integration notes.
[07:22] Diego: On the quantization front, we can run a small perf matrix: int8 vs fp16 vs bf16 across seq lengths 32, 64, 256 and batch sizes 1,4,8. We'll share kernel-level breakdowns (matmul vs decode).
[07:38] Raj: Please do. Also can you run bench with streaming toggled on and off and show both p95/p99 and token throughput?
[07:45] Diego: Yes — that's part of our action items. We'll include packet-level tracing for the bench run so you can see hop-level effects.
[07:55] Tom: What about fallback strategies in case of degraded cross-AZ network? We want graceful degradation rather than errors.
[08:02] Diego: Redwood's runtime supports automatic model variant fallback: if remote variant is slow, route to a smaller local quantized variant or a lower-cost model. Also we can configure timeouts and queue policies to surface partial results for streaming so user experiences degraded but not failed responses.
[08:20] Elena: Are there known quick wins we can apply now?
[08:23] Maya: Yes: (1) increase streaming keepalive and enable HTTP/2 multiplexing where possible, (2) push top-200 prefix warmups during peak startup, (3) move KV read replicas to inference AZs or use mem-attached caches, (4) enable adaptive batching with micro-flush for hot paths.
[08:39] Raj: We'll try warmups + traceroutes first week and share findings.
[08:44] Diego: We'll prepare the bench run config and a sample script to replay p99 traces. Also we'll share the quant matrix and a tuning guide. Link to the lab deck: https://redwood.ai/bench/multipath-cascade-lab (demo link).
[08:58] Lina: For compliance, please include a short note on what runtime caching stores — we need to include that in our audit package.
[09:04] Maya: Will do.
[09:07] Quick recap: Redwood to run benches (streaming on/off), share prefetch script and quant matrix, customer to share traceroutes and topology, follow-up deep-dive week of 2026-01-26.
[09:18] Tom: Thanks all. Good session.
